raw_response:
I've been farming this land in Quzhou my whole adult life. My husband and I have about 10 mu — it's not much, but it's what we have. We do what everyone around here does: wheat in winter, corn in summer. Same rotation, every year. I know this land, I know what it gives back.

For wheat, I'll buy the same improved variety I used last two years — the seed dealer in town sells Jimai 22, my neighbor uses it and gets good yield. I'll do rotary tillage before planting, apply the base fertilizer then top-dress in spring at jointing. I irrigate three times — before winter sets in, then at jointing, then when it heads. Two sprays: one herbicide early spring, one for aphids later. Expect around 450 jin per mu if the rain cooperates.

After wheat harvest in June I'll plant corn right away — no-till, the machine just drops seed into the stubble. Corn is all hybrid, Zhengdan 958 or whatever the seed station has that year. Corn mostly gets summer rain, so I only irrigate once if it's a dry July. Two pesticide passes — one for weeds early on, one for corn borer later.

I don't experiment. Market prices go up and down but wheat and corn always sell. I know the costs, I know the yield, and the work fits what two people can manage.

I use improved wheat varieties (Jimai 22) and hybrid maize (Zhengdan 958 or equivalent) because certified seed from the local dealer is reliable and the yield advantage over saved seed is clear. Fertilizer rates are set at what I know from experience and from watching neighbors — a base application before planting plus a spring top-dress for wheat, and a single split application for maize. Wheat gets three irrigations drawing from the village well network; maize relies mostly on summer monsoon rainfall with one supplemental irrigation if July is dry. Tillage is rotary for wheat to prepare a good seedbed, and no-till direct seeding for maize immediately after wheat harvest to save time and moisture. I grow nothing else — cotton prices have been unpredictable and vegetables need more labor than we have. Wheat and maize are stable income, I know every step of the work, and the whole village does the same so machinery, inputs, and buyers are all easy to access."
